French True Friends: Business

These French business words really do match their English look-alikes, so you can trust them. Each pair below shows both meanings and the small differences worth knowing.

104 word pairs.

information = information (A2)

information (FR) = information; in plural, it can also mean the news.

information (EN) = information.

Useful grammar trap: in English, 'information' is uncountable. Say 'some information,' not 'informations'.

communication = communication (B1)

communication (FR) = communication.

communication (EN) = communication.

The '-tion' bridge is reliable here; English stress falls late: com-mu-ni-KAY-shun.

solution = solution (A2)

solution (FR) = a solution.

solution (EN) = a solution.

Same word in business and science. English stress lands on the middle: so-LOO-shun.

total = total (A2)

total (FR) = total.

total (EN) = total.

A clean true friend for numbers and summaries. English often sounds like TOH-t'l.

international = international (A2)

international (FR) = international.

international (EN) = international.

The prefix 'inter-' works the same way. In fast American English, the 't' may be softened or dropped.

responsable = responsible (B1)

responsable (FR) = in charge or accountable.

responsible (EN) = the same: accountable or in charge.

In French the noun can also mean a manager.

produit = product (A2)

produit = something manufactured, grown, or created for sale.

From Latin 'producere' (to bring forth), both name what is made.

organisation = organization (B1)

organisation = a structured group of people working together.

Same meaning in both languages.

administration = administration (B1)

administration = the management or governance of an organization.

From Latin 'administrare' (to serve, manage), both refer to governance.

économique = economic (B1)

économique = relating to the economy, trade, and production of wealth.

From Greek 'oikonomia' (household management), both kept the resource meaning.

architecture = architecture (B1)

architecture means architecture in both languages.

The oral trap is the ch: in English it sounds like k, as in AR-ki-tek-chur.

document = document (A2)

A key professional true friend. Same written form, same idea: a file, paper, or digital document. English stresses the first syllable: DOC-you-ment.

acte = act (B1)

acte/act = an action, a deed, or a division of a play.

Both also have legal uses: "acte de naissance," "Act of Parliament."

Same meaning in most everyday contexts.

profession = profession (A2)

profession = a skilled occupation requiring specialized training.

From Latin 'professio' (public declaration), both describe a declared career or trade.

président = president (B1)

président = the head of state, company, or organization.

From Latin 'praesidens' (sitting before, presiding), both name the person in charge.

migration = migration (B1)

migration = the movement of people, animals, or data from one place to another.

From Latin 'migrare' (to move), both describe the same displacement.

horizon = horizon (B1)

horizon = the line where earth and sky appear to meet.

From Greek 'horizein' (to limit), both describe the same visual boundary.

promotion = promotion (B1)

promotion (FR) = a career advancement or a marketing campaign; in universities, it can also mean a graduating class.

promotion (EN) = a career advancement or a marketing campaign.

idéal = ideal (B1)

A near-perfect twin: the ideal option in both languages. The main difference is sound: English stresses the middle, as in ai-DEE-al.

challenge = challenge (B1)

A modern true friend. In French business, it means a stimulating challenge. In English, it can also be a verb: to challenge someone.

bonus = bonus (A2)

Same meaning: an extra reward, advantage, or payment. English stretches the first vowel: BOH-nus.

impact = impact (B1)

Same written form, same core meaning: an effect or influence. In professional English, the stress usually comes first: IM-pact.

standard = standard (B1)

Used the same way as a noun or adjective: a standard, a standard process, a standard format. English stresses the first syllable: STAN-dard.

innovation = innovation (B2)

The -tion pattern works perfectly here: same spelling, same meaning. English pronounces the final part like -VAY-shun.

flexibilité = flexibility (B2)

The French suffix -té often becomes English -ty. Flexibilité and flexibility share the same professional meaning: the ability to adapt.

spécialiste = specialist (B1)

The French suffix -iste becomes English -ist. Same role: a specialist in a field, skill, or topic.

négociable = negotiable (B2)

The -able pattern stays transparent. Negotiable means open to discussion or adjustment in both languages.

flexible = flexible (B1)

The -ible ending is transparent here. Same meaning in interviews, project work, and everyday planning: able to adapt.

prioriser = prioritize (B2)

A useful action-verb bridge: French -iser maps to English -ize. Same business meaning: to rank tasks by importance.

optimiser = optimize (B2)

Another -iser to -ize verb. Same professional meaning: to improve a process, tool, or system so it works better.

organiser = organize (A2)

Same action, different ending: organiser becomes organize. English also accepts organise in British spelling.

moderniser = modernize (B1)

The -iser to -ize pattern works again. Modernize is useful in technology and management for updating systems or processes.

visualiser = visualize (B2)

The French -iser ending maps to English -ize. Visualize means to imagine something clearly or display data as a chart or graphic.

personnaliser = personalize (B1)

The -iser to -ize pattern works here too. Personalize is a key marketing and product word: adapt something to a specific user or customer.

standardiser = standardize (B2)

Same structure and same business meaning: to make methods, formats, or rules follow one shared standard.

synchroniser = synchronize (B2)

A transparent technical and business verb. Both languages often shorten it in tech contexts: synchro in French, sync in English.

automatiser = automate (B2)

A small ending shift: French automatiser becomes English automate. Same meaning: make a task run automatically.

adapter = adapt (A2)

adapter (FR) = to adapt, adjust, or make something fit.

adapt (EN) = to change something so it fits a new need.

Safe match: adapter matches adapt; do not confuse it with adopt.

adoption = adoption (B1)

Same spelling and same meaning. It works for adopting a child, but also for adopting a new technology, tool, or strategy.

collaboration = collaboration (B1)

A central teamwork word. Same spelling and same meaning: working together on a shared project or goal.

coordination = coordination (B1)

A perfect project-management twin. Same meaning: making people, tasks, or actions work together in an organized way.

décision = decision (A2)

The accents disappear in English, but the meaning stays the same. Decision is a core business word for choosing between options.

évaluation = evaluation (B2)

The initial accent disappears in English. Same meaning: an assessment, review, or evaluation, including annual performance evaluations.

position = position (A2)

Same word for a physical place, a viewpoint, or a role in a company. In English, it sounds like po-ZI-shun.

production = production (B1)

A true friend across industry, film, and software. In tech, production can mean the live environment: push to production.

protection = protection (B1)

Same spelling, same meaning. Useful in law, cybersecurity, insurance, and human resources: data protection, worker protection.

qualification = qualification (B2)

Same written form and same meaning: a skill, credential, or official requirement. Useful for resumes and job descriptions.

relation = relation (A2)

A transparent word for a connection between people, things, or ideas. In business English, relations is often plural: client relations, public relations.

transformation = transformation (B2)

A key consulting and technology word. Same spelling and same meaning: a major change in form, model, or organization.

transition = transition (B1)

Same spelling and same meaning: a move from one state to another. Useful for energy transition, career transition, or business transition.

version = version (A2)

A perfect tech twin: version means the same thing in both languages. Think V1, V2, beta version, final version.

vision = vision (B1)

Same meaning for eyesight and long-term strategy. In business English, vision often means the direction a leader wants to build toward.

mission = mission (A2)

Same spelling and same meaning: a task, purpose, or company direction. Mission statement is a common business phrase.

conclusion = conclusion (B1)

Same word for the end of a presentation, report, or argument. English stress falls in the middle: con-CLOO-zhun.

discussion = discussion (A2)

Same spelling and same meaning, but often slightly more formal in English: a serious exchange of ideas or points of view.

division = division (B1)

A true friend in math and business. In a company, a division can mean a department, branch, or business unit.

extension = extension (B1)

Same spelling and same meaning. It can mean extra time, a browser extension, a phone extension, or an added part.

inclusion = inclusion (B1)

Same spelling and same meaning. A modern management word, often used in diversity and inclusion.

progression = progression (B1)

Same spelling and same meaning: gradual movement forward, step by step. Useful for progress tracking and performance curves.

application = application (A2)

Transparent and tech-friendly. Both languages shorten it the same way: une appli in French, an app in English.

contribution = contribution (B1)

Same spelling and same meaning: help or value added to a project, team, or result. English stresses the -BYOO- sound: con-tri-BYOO-shun.

distribution = distribution (B1)

A useful true friend in logistics, commerce, and technology. It can describe a distribution chain or a Linux distribution.

installation = installation (A2)

Same spelling and same meaning. Useful for physical equipment, software setup, and technical deployment.

instruction = instruction (B1)

Same word, but business English often uses the plural instructions to mean steps or directions to follow.

intervention = intervention (B2)

Same spelling and same meaning. It can describe speaking in a meeting or a technical visit by an engineer on site.

limitation = limitation (B1)

A perfect true friend for restrictions, technical constraints, or legal limits. English stress falls near the end: lim-i-TAY-shun.

orientation = orientation (B2)

Same spelling, but English business usage often means onboarding or initial training for a new employee.

participation = participation (B1)

Perfectly transparent. Same meaning: taking part in an activity, meeting, project, or decision process.

présentation = presentation (A2)

The accent disappears in English. Same professional meaning: a talk, deck, or meeting presentation.

recommandation = recommendation (B1)

Very close, but watch the middle: French recommandation becomes English recommendation. Same meaning: advice or a formal suggestion.

réduction = reduction (B1)

The accent disappears in English. Same meaning: making something smaller or lower, such as cost reduction or risk reduction.

régulation = regulation (B2)

The accent disappears in English. Same meaning: official rules, legal control, or automatic control of a system.

simulation = simulation (B1)

A perfect written twin. Common in aviation, finance, medicine, training, and video games.

structure = structure (A2)

A perfect written twin. In English, the ending sounds like -cher: STRUK-cher. Useful for company structure, code structure, and document structure.

stratégie = strategy (B1)

French -gie becomes English -gy, and the accent disappears. English stresses the first syllable: STRAT-uh-jee.

méthode = method (A2)

English drops the final -e and the accent. The main oral trap is the th sound in method: place the tongue lightly between the teeth.

processus = process (B1)

French processus becomes the shorter English process. Essential for describing the steps, workflow, or sequence of a project.

prototype = prototype (B2)

Same spelling and same meaning. Very common in tech, design, and industry. English says PRO-tuh-type, with the final type clearly pronounced.

module = module (B1)

Same spelling and same meaning. Used for a training unit or a code component. US English often says MAH-jool; UK English often says MOD-yool.

format = format (A2)

A clean true friend. It works for document size, file type (.pdf, .csv), media format, or meeting structure.

profil = profile (A2)

French profil becomes English profile, with a final silent -e. Useful for a user account, a social media page, or a candidate description.

performance = performance (B1)

Same spelling and same meaning. In business and tech, performance measures how well a person, company, process, or server works.

capacité = capacity (B1)

French -té becomes English -ty. Capacity can mean maximum volume, production ability, storage space, or legal ability.

priorité = priority (B1)

French -té becomes English -ty. A daily management word for what should be handled first.

qualité = quality (A2)

Another -té to -ty pattern. Quality can mean product excellence, quality control, or a positive personal trait.

sécurité = security (A2)

French -té becomes English -ty, and the French accent disappears. Security works for physical safety, road safety, IT security, and cybersecurity.

stabilité = stability (B2)

French -té becomes English -ty. Stability is used for an economy, an infrastructure, a relationship, or reliable software.

visibilité = visibility (B2)

French -té becomes English -ty. In modern business English, visibility means clear access to data, progress, risks, or forecasts.

responsabilité = responsibility (B1)

A long but transparent -ty word. Responsibility is very useful on a CV, in job descriptions, and when defining who owns a task.

diversité = diversity (B1)

French -té becomes English -ty. Diversity is a major workplace concept in modern company culture.

identité = identity (A2)

French -té becomes English -ty. Identity works for official documents and for tech, especially identity and access management.

confidentialité = confidentiality (B2)

A strong -ty pattern. Confidentiality is crucial in law, HR, cybersecurity, and confidentiality agreements.

créativité = creativity (B1)

French -té becomes English -ty, and the accent disappears. Creativity is essential in design, marketing, product work, and innovation.

productivité = productivity (B1)

French -té becomes English -ty, and the accent disappears. Productivity is a key word in business performance analysis.

mobilité = mobility (B1)

French -té becomes English -ty. Mobility can mean transport, internal job moves, or mobile technology.

autorité = authority (B2)

French -té becomes English -ty. Authority can mean legal power, official control, or a recognized expert source. Watch the th sound.

capitalisme = capitalism (B2)

French -isme becomes English -ism. Capitalism has the same meaning: an economic system based on private ownership.

mécanisme = mechanism (B2)

French -isme becomes English -ism. The main trap is pronunciation: the ch in mechanism sounds like k in English.

pragmatisme = pragmatism (C1)

French -isme becomes English -ism. Pragmatism is a valued professional quality: choosing what works in practice over theory.

professionnalisme = professionalism (B1)

French -isme becomes English -ism. Watch the spelling: French professionnalisme has double n; English professionalism has one n.

analyste = analyst (B2)

French -iste becomes English -ist. Analyst is a key role in tech, finance, data, and business reporting.

économiste = economist (B2)

French -iste becomes English -ist, and the accent disappears. Economist stresses the second syllable: e-CON-uh-mist.

accessible = accessible (B1)

The adjective in -ible is spelled the same in both languages. Accessible works for physical access and for content that is easy to understand.

validité = validity (B2)

Final -té to -ty pattern. Validity works for an expiry date, a legal document, a research result, or the logic of an argument.
